The observed difference is not statistically significant and is consistent with random variation. Extending the test duration or increasing the sample size would provide stronger evidence.

The evidence does not support the claim that the new onboarding sequence increases 7-day activation. The observed 1.3 percentage point lift (22.4% vs. 21.1%) is not statistically significant (p = 0.43), indicating the difference is highly likely due to random chance rather than a true effect.

Two design factors further limit reliability. First, running the test during a bank-holiday week introduces external behavioral noise that can distort baseline activation rates. Second, an 8-day test measuring a 7-day metric censors users who signed up on days 2–8, preventing complete observation of their activation window.

Strictly based on this data, there is no evidence of improvement. To draw reliable conclusions, future tests should run long enough to capture full 7-day windows for all cohorts, avoid holiday periods, and be adequately powered to detect the expected effect size.

The evidence does not support the claim that homework-free Fridays improve reading scores. First, the national reading test changed format this year, making year-on-year score comparisons invalid. Second, results were contradictory: scores rose at one school but fell at the other, showing no consistent effect. Third, the sample size is extremely small (two schools over one year), preventing generalization. Parent satisfaction data is irrelevant to academic outcomes and suffers from a low response rate (~33%), introducing potential bias. Without a controlled design, comparable assessment metrics, or a larger sample, any observed changes cannot be causally linked to the intervention. The evidence is inconclusive and methodologically insufficient to determine whether homework-free Fridays impact reading achievement.

Because the new indexes introduce unmeasured write overhead, they may degrade write performance in production, potentially negating read gains. The staging results reflect a specific read workload and noisy tail metrics, not production conditions. To validate production impact, you need write-latency benchmarks at production write ratios, larger tail-latency samples, and isolated testing. Currently, the evidence does not support concluding the new configuration will make production queries faster.

Without isolated runners, larger samples, and cache hit-rate tracking, the observed reduction could easily be random fluctuation. Controlled testing on dedicated infrastructure would be needed to draw a reliable conclusion.
